name: Finnish nationalism
summary: Finnish nationalism is the national movement that grew out of the nineteenth-century Fennoman movement in the Grand Duchy of Finland. Led intellectually by J. V. Snellman, it identified the nation with the Finnish language and culture and set out to unite the Swedish-speaking educated class with the Finnish-speaking peasant majority by making Finnish the language of administration, schooling and culture, building patriotic public education and drawing on the Kalevala and folk tradition. Its defining texts treat the state as the development of a nation's culture and national spirit, prize national independence and self-reliance, and favour cross-class national unity, social conservatism and gradual, lawful change.
scope: As its defining sources set it out: Alapuro's chapter 'Finnish Nationalism' (State and Revolution in Finland) treats it as the nationalism of the Fennoman movement, an interclass, culture-first autonomist nationalism that also served as the civic religion of the Finnish state, whose philosophy of nationality 'received definite expression in Snellman's writings' and was 'refined and extended, but not basically altered, by later Fennomans'; the Encyclopedia of Romantic Nationalism in Europe traces Finnish nationalism from the Turku Romantics through Snellman, Lönnrot's Kalevala and the Finnish Party to its dissolution into modern parties after 1905. It is answered from that scholarship and from Snellman's main work of political philosophy, Valtio-oppi (Läran om staten, 1842), used where it sets out his theory of nationality, patriotism and the national state (the nation, its language and schools, its classes and trade, and its sovereignty, wars and relations with other nations). Modern parties that call themselves nationalist, such as the Finns Party, are other subjects and are not used; nor are the Greater Finland and Lapua strands, which the scholarship mentions but for which no defining text was found. Silence in these sources is left null.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-08), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-20) answered from five Wikipedia articles, the Finns Party's English page and the Kalevala; under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence and a party is another subject, so every one of its answers was re-answered from the defining scholarship and Snellman's Valtio-oppi or nulled, with the first version kept in each statement's reviewHistory (s1-s7 stay listed for that history and for the first pass's missing statements). Valtio-oppi is read in the Finnish translation of the Snellman-instituutti collected works; it is used only where it states Snellman's theory of nationality and the national state, not for his general legal philosophy (marriage, juries, punishment, press law), which the defining sources do not tie to Finnish nationalism. Themes searched: culture and society (Alapuro, ERNiE, Valtio-oppi sections 2-6, 13), economy (Valtio-oppi sections 33-39 on classes, trade and tariffs; Alapuro on the peasantry), government (Valtio-oppi sections 52-65 on sovereignty, forms of government, estates and suffrage), world (Valtio-oppi sections 65-67 on war, alliances and international law), means (Alapuro, Valtio-oppi on lawful reform), religion (Valtio-oppi section 6). Nothing found on ecology or technology beyond the Fennomans' defence of agrarian society, on welfare, family, gender or criminal justice as part of the nationalist programme, or on immigration. Local corpora checked: the Gutenberg catalog has Yrjö-Koskinen's and Julius Krohn's books only as fiction and history in Finnish, no programme; the reference library and the parliamentary corpora hold no Finnish nationalist texts. Not reached: the University of Turku repository (utupub.fi, 403) for Jalava's and others' work on Snellman; Fewster's Visions of Past Glory has no open full text in HELDA; Britannica's Snellman entry was not used (blocked for scripted access). The interwar Academic Karelia Society, the Lapua movement and the Greater Finland idea, which Alapuro calls nationalist, are left out for want of a defining text tying their programmes to Finnish nationalism as such.
